claim: Adolescents are especially prone to drug addiction.
source: Adolescents are especially prone to drug addiction, but the underlying biological basis of their increased vulnerability remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The underlying biological basis of adolescent increased vulnerability to drug addiction remains unknown.
source: Adolescents are especially prone to drug addiction, but the underlying biological basis of their increased vulnerability remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: Translational control by phosphorylation of eIF2α accounts for adolescent hypersensitivity to cocaine.
source: We reveal that translational control by phosphorylation of the translation initiation factor eIF2α (p-eIF2α) accounts for adolescent hypersensitivity to cocaine.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study supported by multiple experimental results throughout the manuscript.

claim: In adolescent mice, a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) reduced p-eIF2α in the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
source: In adolescent (but not adult) mice, a low dose of cocaine reduced p-eIF2α in the ventral tegmental area (VTA), potentiated synaptic inputs to VTA dopaminergic neurons, and induced drug-reinforced behavior.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2a-b.

claim: In adolescent mice, a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) potentiated synaptic inputs to VTA dopaminergic neurons.
source: In adolescent (but not adult) mice, a low dose of cocaine reduced p-eIF2α in the ventral tegmental area (VTA), potentiated synaptic inputs to VTA dopaminergic neurons, and induced drug-reinforced behavior.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data showing increased AMPAR/NMDAR ratio in Figure 1a.

claim: In adolescent mice, a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) induced drug-reinforced behavior.
source: In adolescent (but not adult) mice, a low dose of cocaine reduced p-eIF2α in the ventral tegmental area (VTA), potentiated synaptic inputs to VTA dopaminergic neurons, and induced drug-reinforced behavior.
evidence: This is supported by CPP behavioral data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Adult mice with reduced p-eIF2α-mediated translational control are more susceptible to cocaine-induced synaptic potentiation.
source: Like adolescents, adult mice with reduced p-eIF2α-mediated translational control were more susceptible to cocaine-induced synaptic potentiation and behavior.
evidence: This is supported by data from Eif2s1S/A mice and ISRIB-treated mice shown in Figure 3.

claim: Adult mice with reduced p-eIF2α-mediated translational control are more susceptible to cocaine-induced behavior.
source: Like adolescents, adult mice with reduced p-eIF2α-mediated translational control were more susceptible to cocaine-induced synaptic potentiation and behavior.
evidence: This is supported by CPP data from Eif2s1S/A mice and ISRIB-treated mice shown in Figure 3.

claim: Adolescent mice with increased p-eIF2α became more resistant to cocaine's effects.
source: Conversely, like adults, adolescent mice with increased p-eIF2α became more resistant to cocaine's effects.
evidence: This is supported by data from Sal003-treated adolescent mice shown in Figure 4.

claim: mGluR-LTD was impaired in adolescent mice.
source: Accordingly, metabotropic glutamate receptor-mediated long-term depression (mGluR-LTD)—whose disruption is postulated to increase vulnerability to drug addiction—was impaired in both adolescent mice and adult mice with reduced p-eIF2α mediated translation.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data showing lack of DHPG-induced LTD in adolescent mice in Figure 1e.

claim: mGluR-LTD was impaired in adult mice with reduced p-eIF2α mediated translation.
source: Accordingly, metabotropic glutamate receptor-mediated long-term depression (mGluR-LTD)—whose disruption is postulated to increase vulnerability to drug addiction—was impaired in both adolescent mice and adult mice with reduced p-eIF2α mediated translation.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data from Eif2s1S/A mice and ISRIB-treated mice shown in Figure 3e-f.

claim: Disruption of mGluR-LTD is postulated to increase vulnerability to drug addiction.
source: Accordingly, metabotropic glutamate receptor-mediated long-term depression (mGluR-LTD)—whose disruption is postulated to increase vulnerability to drug addiction—was impaired in both adolescent mice and adult mice with reduced p-eIF2α mediated translation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: During addiction, cocaine hijacks translational control by p-eIF2α, initiating synaptic potentiation and addiction-related behaviors.
source: Thus, during addiction, cocaine hijacks translational control by p-eIF2α, initiating synaptic potentiation and addiction-related behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: In humans, adolescence is a period of heightened susceptibility to drug addiction.
source: In humans, adolescence is a period of heightened susceptibility to drug addiction (Chambers et al., 2003; Kandel et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The biological basis of heightened vulnerability to substance abuse during adolescence remains elusive.
source: Although some molecular and cellular adaptations associated with drug use have been identified (Bowers et al., 2010; Lüscher and Malenka, 2011), the biological basis of heightened vulnerability to substance abuse during adolescence remains elusive.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap supported by citations.

claim: Addictive drugs hijack the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying long-term changes in synaptic strength in the mesocorticolimbic dopamine system.
source: Converging evidence supports the notion that addictive drugs hijack the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying long-term changes in synaptic strength in the mesocorticolimbic dopamine (DA) system (including the ventral tegmental area (VTA), a key brain reward area implicated in the development of addiction (Kauer, 2004)) in a way that reinforces drug-seeking behavior (Bowers et al., 2010; Kauer and Malenka, 2007; Hyman et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The VTA is a key brain reward area implicated in the development of addiction.
source: Converging evidence supports the notion that addictive drugs hijack the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying long-term changes in synaptic strength in the mesocorticolimbic dopamine (DA) system (including the ventral tegmental area (VTA), a key brain reward area implicated in the development of addiction (Kauer, 2004)) in a way that reinforces drug-seeking behavior (Bowers et al., 2010; Kauer and Malenka, 2007; Hyman et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kauer, 2004.

claim: Addiction has both initiation and maintenance phases.
source: Addiction has both initiation and maintenance phases (Lüscher and Malenka, 2011; Wise and Koob, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Drugs of abuse (including cocaine, amphetamine, nicotine, ethanol, and morphine) all induce long-term potentiation (LTP) of excitatory synapses on VTA DA neurons that lasts for several days after exposure.
source: For instance, drugs of abuse (including cocaine, amphetamine, nicotine, ethanol, and morphine) all induce long-term potentiation (LTP) of excitatory synapses on VTA DA neurons that lasts for several days after exposure (Bowers et al., 2010; Lammel et al., 2014; Ungless et al., 2001; Saal et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Drug-induced LTP results from the insertion of α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs) in the postsynaptic membrane.
source: This LTP, resulting from the insertion of α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs) in the postsynaptic membrane, is measured by recording glutamatergic synaptic currents (EPSCs) at positive holding potentials, and is manifested as an increase in the AMPAR/N-methyl D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) ratio (Ungless et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ungless et al., 2001.

claim: Drug-induced LTP is measured by recording glutamatergic synaptic currents (EPSCs) at positive holding potentials, and is manifested as an increase in the AMPAR/NMDAR ratio.
source: This LTP, resulting from the insertion of α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs) in the postsynaptic membrane, is measured by recording glutamatergic synaptic currents (EPSCs) at positive holding potentials, and is manifested as an increase in the AMPAR/N-methyl D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) ratio (Ungless et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ungless et al., 2001.

claim: mGluR-LTD results from the removal of postsynaptic AMPARs.
source: Furthermore, metabotropic glutamate receptor-mediated long-term depression (mGluR-LTD), resulting from the removal of postsynaptic AMPARs, blocks cocaine-induced LTP in VTA DA neurons (Bellone and Lüscher, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bellone and Lüscher, 2006.

claim: mGluR-LTD blocks cocaine-induced LTP in VTA DA neurons.
source: Furthermore, metabotropic glutamate receptor-mediated long-term depression (mGluR-LTD), resulting from the removal of postsynaptic AMPARs, blocks cocaine-induced LTP in VTA DA neurons (Bellone and Lüscher, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bellone and Lüscher, 2006.

claim: Impaired mGluR-LTD increases vulnerability to drugs of abuse.
source: Thus, it has been postulated that impaired mGluR-LTD increases vulnerability to drugs of abuse (Bellone and Lüscher, 2006; Lüscher and Huber, 2010; Loweth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Protein synthesis is required for cocaine-induced LTP in VTA DA neurons.
source: In VTA DA neurons, protein synthesis is required for cocaine-induced LTP (Argilli et al., 2008; Yuan et al., 2013) and mGluR-LTD (Mameli et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Argilli et al., 2008 and Yuan et al., 2013.

claim: Protein synthesis is required for mGluR-LTD in VTA DA neurons.
source: In VTA DA neurons, protein synthesis is required for cocaine-induced LTP (Argilli et al., 2008; Yuan et al., 2013) and mGluR-LTD (Mameli et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mameli et al., 2007.

claim: Protein synthesis is required for cocaine-induced behaviors.
source: In addition, protein synthesis is also required for cocaine-induced behaviors (Sorg and Ulibarri, 1995; Kuo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sorg and Ulibarri, 1995 and Kuo et al., 2007.

claim: Initiation is the rate limiting step of protein synthesis and a major target for translational control.
source: Initiation is the rate limiting step and a major target for translational control (Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009; Buffington et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009 and Buffington et al., 2014.

claim: Translation initiation is controlled by regulation of the eIF4F complex via mTORC1.
source: The first is by regulation of the eIF4F complex via the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about translational control mechanisms.

claim: Translation initiation is controlled by regulating ternary complex formation via phosphorylation of eIF2α.
source: The second mechanism is by regulating ternary complex formation via phosphorylation of the translation initiation factor eIF2α.
evidence: This is established knowledge about translational control mechanisms.

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2α blocks general translation.
source: Phosphorylation of eIF2α blocks general translation, but also results in translational up-regulation of a small subset of select mRNAs that contain upstream open reading frames (uORFs) in their 5' untranslated region (5'UTR) (Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009; Buffington et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009 and Buffington et al., 2014.

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2α results in translational up-regulation of a small subset of select mRNAs that contain upstream open reading frames (uORFs) in their 5' untranslated region (5'UTR).
source: Phosphorylation of eIF2α blocks general translation, but also results in translational up-regulation of a small subset of select mRNAs that contain upstream open reading frames (uORFs) in their 5' untranslated region (5'UTR) (Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009; Buffington et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009 and Buffington et al., 2014.

claim: Drugs of abuse selectively hijack the translational program controlled by phosphorylation of eIF2α in the VTA.
source: In particular, we show that drugs of abuse selectively hijack the translational program controlled by phosphorylation of eIF2α in the VTA, thus potentiating synaptic inputs to VTA DA neurons and drug-induced behaviors.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: In adolescent mice, a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg i.p.) elicited LTP, manifested by an increase in the AMPAR/NMDAR ratio.
source: In adolescent ) mice, a relatively low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg i.p.) elicited LTP, manifested by an increase in the AMPAR/NMDAR ratio (Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: In adult mice, only higher doses of cocaine (10 and 20 mg/kg) induced LTP in VTA DA neurons.
source: By contrast, only higher doses of cocaine (10 and 20 mg/kg) induced LTP in VTA DA neurons from adult mice (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Cocaine-induced LTP in VTA DA neurons is facilitated in slices from adolescent mice.
source: Thus, cocaine-induced LTP in VTA DA neurons is facilitated in slices from adolescent mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dose-response data comparing adolescent and adult mice.

claim: A low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) elicited CPP in adolescent mice.
source: Strikingly, we found that enhanced LTP in the VTA was mirrored in the behavior of adolescent mice: low doses of cocaine (5 mg/kg) elicited CPP only in adolescents, but not in adult mice (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by CPP behavioral data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: A low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) did not elicit CPP in adult mice.
source: Strikingly, we found that enhanced LTP in the VTA was mirrored in the behavior of adolescent mice: low doses of cocaine (5 mg/kg) elicited CPP only in adolescents, but not in adult mice (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by CPP behavioral data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Higher doses of cocaine (10 mg/kg) were required to induce CPP in adult mice.
source: Further mirroring the LTP results, higher doses of cocaine (10 mg/kg) were required to induce CPP in adult mice (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by CPP behavioral data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Adolescent mice are more sensitive to the effects of cocaine with regard to both synaptic transmission and behavior.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that adolescent mice are more sensitive to the effects of cocaine with regard to both synaptic transmission and behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the LTP and CPP data comparing adolescent and adult mice.

claim: In slices from adolescent mice, a relatively low concentration of cocaine (1 μM) elicited LTP in VTA DA neurons.
source: In slices from adolescent mice, a relatively low concentration of cocaine (1 μM) elicited LTP in VTA DA neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b), whereas in slices from adult mice only a higher concentration of cocaine (5 μM) induced LTP (Figure 1—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b.

claim: In slices from adult mice, only a higher concentration of cocaine (5 μM) induced LTP.
source: In slices from adolescent mice, a relatively low concentration of cocaine (1 μM) elicited LTP in VTA DA neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b), whereas in slices from adult mice only a higher concentration of cocaine (5 μM) induced LTP (Figure 1—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3c.

claim: The concentrations of cocaine in both blood and brain are similar in adolescent and adult mice.
source: Taken together with previous reports that the concentrations of cocaine in both blood and brain are similar in adolescent and adult mice (Zombeck et al., 2009), these data support the notion that cocaine-induced LTP in VTA DA neurons has a lower threshold in adolescent mice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zombeck et al., 2009.

claim: Cocaine-induced LTP in VTA DA neurons has a lower threshold in adolescent mice.
source: Taken together with previous reports that the concentrations of cocaine in both blood and brain are similar in adolescent and adult mice (Zombeck et al., 2009), these data support the notion that cocaine-induced LTP in VTA DA neurons has a lower threshold in adolescent mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro cocaine application data and previous literature.

claim: DHPG induced LTD in VTA DA neurons from adult mice.
source: In agreement with this prediction, a brief-application of DHPG—a selective mGluR1/5 agonist—induced LTD in VTA DA neurons from adult (Figure 1e), but not adolescent mice (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: DHPG did not induce LTD in VTA DA neurons from adolescent mice.
source: In agreement with this prediction, a brief-application of DHPG—a selective mGluR1/5 agonist—induced LTD in VTA DA neurons from adult (Figure 1e), but not adolescent mice (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Translation rates in the brain decrease significantly with age.
source: Given that translation rates in the brain decrease significantly with age (Vargas and Castaneda, 1983), we examined whether a low dose of cocaine is sufficient to trigger LTP in VTA DA neurons and induce CPP in adolescent mice (Figure 1a and 1c) also activates a particular translational control program in the VTA of these mice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vargas and Castaneda, 1983.

claim: A low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) reduced the amount of phosphorylated eIF2α (p-eIF2α) only in VTA slices from adolescent mice.
source: We found that a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) reduced the amount of phosphorylated eIF2α (p-eIF2α) only in VTA slices from adolescent mice (Figure 2a and 2b).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2a and 2b.

claim: A higher dose of cocaine (10 mg/kg) was required to decrease p-eIF2α levels in VTA slices from adult mice.
source: By contrast, a higher dose of cocaine (10 mg/kg) was required to decrease p-eIF2α levels in VTA slices from adult mice (Figure 2a and 2b).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2a and 2b.

claim: A single injection of cocaine failed to alter p-eIF2α levels in the nucleus accumbens.
source: Importantly, a signle injection of cocaine failed to alter p-eIF2α levels in the nucleus accumbens (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), another brain region involved in addiction (Kalivas and Volkow, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The nucleus accumbens is a brain region involved in addiction.
source: Importantly, a signle injection of cocaine failed to alter p-eIF2α levels in the nucleus accumbens (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), another brain region involved in addiction (Kalivas and Volkow, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kalivas and Volkow, 2011.

claim: A low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) did not significantly alter phosphorylation of S6K at Thr-389 in adolescent mice.
source: In abilescnt mice, a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) did not significantly alter phosphorylation of S6K at Thr-389 (d), 4E-BP1 at Thr-37 and Thr-46 (e) and eIF4E at Ser209 (f).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: A low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) did not significantly alter phosphorylation of 4E-BP1 at Thr-37 and Thr-46 in adolescent mice.
source: In abilescnt mice, a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) did not significantly alter phosphorylation of S6K at Thr-389 (d), 4E-BP1 at Thr-37 and Thr-46 (e) and eIF4E at Ser209 (f).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: A low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) did not significantly alter phosphorylation of eIF4E at Ser209 in adolescent mice.
source: In abilescnt mice, a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) did not significantly alter phosphorylation of S6K at Thr-389 (d), 4E-BP1 at Thr-37 and Thr-46 (e) and eIF4E at Ser209 (f).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: eIF2α is a newly identified effector of cocaine action.
source: Thus, eIF2α is a newly identified effector of cocaine action.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing cocaine's selective effect on eIF2α phosphorylation.

claim: In Eif2s1S/A mutant mice, eIF2α phosphorylation was significantly reduced in the VTA.
source: In Eif2s1S/A mutant mice, eIF2α phosphorylation was significantly reduced in the VTA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) induced LTP in VTA DA neurons from Eif2s1S/A mutant mice but not in VTA DA neurons from WT littermates.
source: As predicted, a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) induced LTP in VTA DA neurons from Eif2s1S/A mutant mice but not in VTA DA neurons from WT littermates (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Application of a low concentration of cocaine (1 μM) in vitro was sufficient to induce LTP in VTA DA neurons from Eif2s1S/A mutant mice, but not in those from adult WT controls.
source: In addition, application of a low concentration of cocaine (1 μM) in vitro was sufficient to induce LTP in VTA DA neurons from Eif2s1S/A mutant mice, but not in those from adult WT controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Low doses of cocaine (5 mg/kg) induced CPP only in Eif2s1S/A mutant mice.
source: Consistent with the LTP results, low doses of cocaine (5 mg/kg) induced CPP only in Eif2s1S/A mutant mice (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by CPP behavioral data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Like adolescent mice, adult mice with reduced p-eIF2α are more susceptible to cocaine-evoked LTP (both in vivo and in vitro) and drug-induced behavior.
source: Hence, like adolescent mice, adult mice with reduced p-eIF2α are more susceptible to cocaine-evoked LTP (both in vivo and in vitro) and drug-induced behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data on Eif2s1S/A mutant mice.

claim: ISRIB is a small molecule inhibitor that potently blocks p-eIF2α-mediated translational effects by promoting eIF2B activity.
source: We therefore used a recently-discovered small molecule inhibitor ISRIB (Sidrauski et al., 2013), which potently blocks p-eIF2α-mediated translational effects by promoting eIF2B activity (Sekine et al., 2015; Sidrauski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sidrauski et al., 2013, Sekine et al., 2015, and Sidrauski et al., 2015.

claim: Adult WT mice injected with ISRIB (2.5 mg/kg) and a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) showed both LTP in VTA and drug-induced CPP.
source: Adult WT mice injected with ISRIB (2.5 mg/kg) and a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) showed both LTP in VTA (Figure 3c) and drug-induced CPP (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology and behavioral data shown in Figure 3c and 3d.

claim: Neither cocaine nor ISRIB alone triggered LTP or CPP in adult WT mice.
source: Note that neither cocaine nor ISRIB alone triggered LTP or CPP in adult WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by control data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Reduced p-eIF2α–mediated translational control renders adult mice more susceptible to the synaptic and behavioral effects of cocaine.
source: These results support the notion that reduced p-eIF2α–mediated translational control renders adult mice more susceptible to the synaptic and behavioral effects of cocaine.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ISRIB experiments.

claim: mGluR-LTD was impaired in VTA DA neurons from mice with reduced p-eIF2α (Eif2s1S/A mice).
source: Consistent with this prediction, mGluR-LTD was impaired in VTA DA neurons from mice with reduced p-eIF2α (Eif2s1S/A mice) and adult WT mice injected with ISRIB (Figure 3e–f).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3e-f.

claim: mGluR-LTD was impaired in adult WT mice injected with ISRIB.
source: Consistent with this prediction, mGluR-LTD was impaired in VTA DA neurons from mice with reduced p-eIF2α (Eif2s1S/A mice) and adult WT mice injected with ISRIB (Figure 3e–f).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3e-f.

claim: Parallel genetic and pharmacological experiments provide strong evidence that reducing p-eIF2α-mediated translational control in the VTA of adult mice makes them more like adolescents with respect to mGluR-LTD, and cocaine-evoked LTP and CPP.
source: Thus, our parallel genetic and pharmacological experiments provide strong evidence that reducing p-eIF2α-mediated translational control in the VTA of adult mice makes them more like adolescents with respect to mGluR-LTD, and cocaine-evoked LTP and CPP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined genetic and pharmacological data.

claim: Sal003 is an inhibitor of eIF2α phosphatases.
source: To examine whether increasing p-eIF2α in the VTA of adolescent mice is sufficient to confer resistance to low doses of cocaine, we administered Sal003, an inhibitor of eIF2α phosphatases (Boyce et al., 2005; Robert et al., 2006) (Figure 4a and 4b), directly into the VTA of young mice to promote eIF2α phosphorylation locally (Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boyce et al., 2005 and Robert et al., 2006.

claim: A low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) induced LTP in adolescent mice locally infused with vehicle.
source: As expected, a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) induced LTP in adolescent mice locally infused with vehicle (Figure 4b), but not in VTA DA neurons from adolescent mice infused with Sal003 (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: A low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) did not induce LTP in VTA DA neurons from adolescent mice infused with Sal003.
source: As expected, a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) induced LTP in adolescent mice locally infused with vehicle (Figure 4b), but not in VTA DA neurons from adolescent mice infused with Sal003 (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The Sal003-mediated increase in p-eIF2α blocked the LTP evoked by cocaine in vitro in brain slices.
source: The Sal003-mediated increase in p-eIF2α also blocked the LTP evoked by cocaine in vitro in brain slices (Figure 4d–e), further supporting the in vivo experiments.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4d-e.

claim: Low doses of cocaine elicited CPP in vehicle-infused but not in Sal003-infused adolescent mice.
source: Low doses of cocaine elicited CPP in vehicle-infused but not in Sal003-infused adolescent mice (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by CPP behavioral data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Sal003 induced mGluR-LTD in VTA slices from adolescent mice.
source: Moreover, as expected, Sal003 induced mGluR-LTD in VTA slices from adolescent mice (Figure 4g).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: A direct increase in p-eIF2α in the VTA of adolescent mice blocks the susceptibility to cocaine-induced LTP and behavior by promoting an opposing LTD in VTA DA neurons.
source: Hence, a direct increase in p-eIF2α in the VTA of adolescent mice blocks the susceptibility to cocaine-induced LTP and behavior by promoting an opposing LTD in VTA DA neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Sal003 experiments.

claim: eIF2α phosphorylation-mediated translational control is both necessary and sufficient for mGluR-LTD in the hippocampus.
source: Given that a) eIF2α phosphorylation-mediated translational control is both necessary and sufficient for mGluR-LTD in the hippocampus (Di Prisco et al., 2014) and VTA (Figures 3e, f and 4g), b) eIF2α phosphorylation blocks general translation but selectively triggers translation of a few select mRNAs during mGluR-LTD (including oligrophrenin-1 (Ophn1) mRNA) (Di Prisco et al., 2014), and c) translation of Ophn1 mRNA is required for mGluR-LTD (Di Prisco et al., 2014; Nadif Kasri et al., 2011), we predicted that in adult mice with reduced OPHN1 levels in VTA, a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) would induce LTP and CPP.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Di Prisco et al., 2014.

claim: eIF2α phosphorylation-mediated translational control is both necessary and sufficient for mGluR-LTD in the VTA.
source: Given that a) eIF2α phosphorylation-mediated translational control is both necessary and sufficient for mGluR-LTD in the hippocampus (Di Prisco et al., 2014) and VTA (Figures 3e, f and 4g), b) eIF2α phosphorylation blocks general translation but selectively triggers translation of a few select mRNAs during mGluR-LTD (including oligrophrenin-1 (Ophn1) mRNA) (Di Prisco et al., 2014), and c) translation of Ophn1 mRNA is required for mGluR-LTD (Di Prisco et al., 2014; Nadif Kasri et al., 2011), we predicted that in adult mice with reduced OPHN1 levels in VTA, a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) would induce LTP and CPP.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3e, f and 4g.

claim: eIF2α phosphorylation selectively triggers translation of oligrophrenin-1 (Ophn1) mRNA during mGluR-LTD.
source: Given that a) eIF2α phosphorylation-mediated translational control is both necessary and sufficient for mGluR-LTD in the hippocampus (Di Prisco et al., 2014) and VTA (Figures 3e, f and 4g), b) eIF2α phosphorylation blocks general translation but selectively triggers translation of a few select mRNAs during mGluR-LTD (including oligrophrenin-1 (Ophn1) mRNA) (Di Prisco et al., 2014), and c) translation of Ophn1 mRNA is required for mGluR-LTD (Di Prisco et al., 2014; Nadif Kasri et al., 2011), we predicted that in adult mice with reduced OPHN1 levels in VTA, a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) would induce LTP and CPP.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Di Prisco et al., 2014.

claim: Translation of Ophn1 mRNA is required for mGluR-LTD.
source: Given that a) eIF2α phosphorylation-mediated translational control is both necessary and sufficient for mGluR-LTD in the hippocampus (Di Prisco et al., 2014) and VTA (Figures 3e, f and 4g), b) eIF2α phosphorylation blocks general translation but selectively triggers translation of a few select mRNAs during mGluR-LTD (including oligrophrenin-1 (Ophn1) mRNA) (Di Prisco et al., 2014), and c) translation of Ophn1 mRNA is required for mGluR-LTD (Di Prisco et al., 2014; Nadif Kasri et al., 2011), we predicted that in adult mice with reduced OPHN1 levels in VTA, a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) would induce LTP and CPP.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Di Prisco et al., 2014 and Nadif Kasri et al., 2011.

claim: In adult mice injected with Ophn1-shRNA in the VTA, a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) triggered LTP in the VTA in vivo.
source: As anticipated, in adult mice injected with a specific shRNA against Ophn1 (Ophn1-shRNA) in the VTA, this low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) triggered LTP in the VTA in vivo (Figure 5a) and induced CPP (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: In adult mice injected with Ophn1-shRNA in the VTA, a low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) induced CPP.
source: As anticipated, in adult mice injected with a specific shRNA against Ophn1 (Ophn1-shRNA) in the VTA, this low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) triggered LTP in the VTA in vivo (Figure 5a) and induced CPP (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by CPP behavioral data shown in Figure 5c (note: the text refers to Figure 5c but the figure shows this as 5b).

claim: A low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) failed to induce LTP in mice injected with a control (scrambled) shRNA.
source: However, the same low dose of cocaine failed to do so in mice injected with a control (scrambled) shRNA (Figure 5a and 5b).
evidence: This is supported by control data shown in Figure 5a and 5b.

claim: A low dose of cocaine (5 mg/kg) failed to induce CPP in mice injected with a control (scrambled) shRNA.
source: However, the same low dose of cocaine failed to do so in mice injected with a control (scrambled) shRNA (Figure 5a and 5b).
evidence: This is supported by control data shown in Figure 5a and 5b.

claim: Like adolescent mice or adult mice with reduced p-eIF2α–mediated translation, adult mice with reduced OPHN1 levels in the VTA are more sensitive to the effects of cocaine.
source: Hence, like adolescent mice (Figure 1a and 1c) or adult mice with reduced p-eIF2α–mediated translation (Figure 3a and 3b), adult mice with reduced OPHN1 levels in the VTA are more sensitive to the effects of cocaine.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the OPHN1 knockdown experiments.

claim: Sal003 blocked cocaine-induced LTP in control VTA DA neurons.
source: Remarkably, Sal003 blocked cocaine-induced LTP in control VTA DA neurons, but not in VTA DA neurons in which OPHN1 was reduced by Ophn1-shRNA (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Sal003 did not block cocaine-induced LTP in VTA DA neurons in which OPHN1 was reduced by Ophn1-shRNA.
source: Remarkably, Sal003 blocked cocaine-induced LTP in control VTA DA neurons, but not in VTA DA neurons in which OPHN1 was reduced by Ophn1-shRNA (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: In vivo injections of cocaine induce LTP in the VTA by replacing postsynaptic AMPARs containing the GluR2 subunit with calcium-permeable AMPARs lacking the GluR2 subunit.
source: In vivo injections of cocaine are known to induce LTP in the VTA by replacing postsynaptic AMPARs containing the GluR2 subunit with calcium-permeable AMPARs lacking the GluR2 subunit (Bellone and Lüscher, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bellone and Lüscher, 2006.

claim: Sal003 blocked the increased inward rectification induced by in vitro application of cocaine in WT slices.
source: We recorded EPSCs at -70, 0 and +40 mV to calculate the rectification index and found that Sal003 blocked the increased inward rectification induced by in vitro application of cocaine in WT slices, but not in slices from OPHN1-deficient mice (Figure 5d–g).
evidence: This is supported by rectification index data shown in Figure 5d-g.

claim: Sal003 did not block the increased inward rectification induced by in vitro application of cocaine in slices from OPHN1-deficient mice.
source: We recorded EPSCs at -70, 0 and +40 mV to calculate the rectification index and found that Sal003 blocked the increased inward rectification induced by in vitro application of cocaine in WT slices, but not in slices from OPHN1-deficient mice (Figure 5d–g).
evidence: This is supported by rectification index data shown in Figure 5d-g.

claim: OPHN1 is a specific target by which eIF2α phosphorylation regulates plasticity changes in VTA DA neurons.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that OPHN1 is a specific target by which eIF2α phosphorylation regulates plasticity changes in VTA DA neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the OPHN1 knockdown and Sal003 experiments.

claim: Different drugs of abuse induce LTP in VTA DA neurons through their actions on distinct receptors.
source: Through their actions on distinct receptors, different drugs of abuse induce LTP in VTA DA neurons, thus reinforcing drug-seeking behavior (Bowers et al., 2010; Lüscher and Malenka, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bowers et al., 2010 and Lüscher and Malenka, 2011.

claim: Methamphetamine, nicotine, and ethanol at doses known to evoke LTP in VTA DA neurons all reduced p-eIF2α in VTA of adult mice.
source: We found that, like cocaine, these drugs with very different mechanisms of action, all reduced p-eIF2α in VTA of adult mice (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Compared to the brains of adolescent mice, protein synthesis is reduced in the brains of adult mice.
source: Compared to the brains of adolescent mice—which are more vulnerable to drugs of abuse—protein synthesis is reduced in the brains of adult mice (Vargas and Castaneda, 1983; Hovda et al., 2006; Sun et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vargas and Castaneda, 1983; Hovda et al., 2006; Sun et al., 1995.

claim: Translational control of gene expression is the ultimate step in the functional output of gene expression.
source: Furthermore, translational control of gene expression is the ultimate step in the functional output of gene expression (Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009) and neurons could regulate protein synthesis without altering mRNA synthesis or transport, allowing for local control of protein synthesis at synapses (Holt and Schuman, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009.

claim: Neurons could regulate protein synthesis without altering mRNA synthesis or transport, allowing for local control of protein synthesis at synapses.
source: Furthermore, translational control of gene expression is the ultimate step in the functional output of gene expression (Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009) and neurons could regulate protein synthesis without altering mRNA synthesis or transport, allowing for local control of protein synthesis at synapses (Holt and Schuman, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holt and Schuman, 2013.

claim: There was no significant difference in the baseline phosphorylation of eIF2α between adolescent and adult mice.
source: It is noteworthy that we could not detect a significant difference in the baseline phosphorylation of eIF2α between adolescent and adult mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Reduced p-eIF2α-mediated translation of Ophn1 mRNA accounts for the adolescent hypersensitivity to cocaine.
source: Collectively, our data indicate that reduced p-eIF2α-mediated translation of Ophn1 mRNA accounts for the adolescent hypersensitivity to cocaine.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data.

claim: Cocaine induces LTP at VTA DA synapses by inserting new AMPARs into the postsynaptic membrane.
source: Cocaine induces LTP at VTA DA synapses by inserting new AMPARs into the postsynaptic membrane (Ungless et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ungless et al., 2001.

claim: Pharmacological or synaptic induction of mGluR-LTD in VTA reverses cocaine-induced LTP by removing AMPARs from the post-synaptic DA neurons.
source: This process is reversed either by pharmacological or synaptic induction of mGluR-LTD in VTA by removing AMPARs from the post-synaptic DA neurons (Bellone and Lüscher, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bellone and Lüscher, 2006.

claim: Reduced mGluR-LTD in the midbrain is postulated to enhance vulnerability to drug addiction.
source: Conversely, reduced mGluR-LTD in the midbrain is postulated to enhance vulnerability to drug addiction (Lüscher and Huber, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lüscher and Huber, 2010.

claim: p-eIF2α-mediated translational control of OPHN1 synthesis is a key mechanism underlying the reversal of cocaine-evoked LTP by mGluR-LTD.
source: Our data provide the first compelling mechanistic evidence that p-eIF2α-mediated translational control of OPHN1 synthesis is a key mechanism underlying the reversal of cocaine-evoked LTP by mGluR-LTD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Blocking mGluR function in the VTA renders cocaine-evoked LTP more long-lasting.
source: Given that blocking mGluR function in the VTA renders cocaine-evoked LTP more long-lasting (Mameli et al., 2009), it will be interesting to determine whether decreasing p-eIF2α also leads to a persistent LTP in the VTA.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mameli et al., 2009.

claim: Drugs of abuse that act on distinct receptors (cocaine, methamphetamine, nicotine and ethanol) all reduce p-eIF2α in the VTA.
source: It is therefore significant that drugs of abuse that act on distinct receptors (cocaine, methamphetamine, nicotine and ethanol), and induce LTP (Bowers et al., 2010; Lüscher and Malenka, 2011) in VTA DA neurons, all reduce p-eIF2α in the VTA (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Five week-old mice (35–42 postnatal days) were selected as adolescents.
source: We therefore selected five week-old mice (35–42 postnatal days) as adolescents, and 3–5 month old mice as adults.
evidence: This is a methodological choice based on developmental characteristics.

claim: During mid-adolescence (postnatal day 35–40), mice show characteristic behavior patterns, including impulsiveness and risk-taking.
source: During mid-adolescence (postnatal day 35–40) (Spear, 2000; Laviola et al., 2003), mice show characteristic behavior patterns, including impulsiveness and risk-taking (Laviola et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Spear, 2000 and Laviola et al., 2003.
